catalog_quote: Perceived stress patterns based on the hundreds of tokens elicited from all nine speakers are clear and consistent. Disyllabic non-verbs (nouns, adjectives, and numerals) are stressed on the second syllable (σ2), and disyllabic verbs are stressed on the first syllable (σ1). ... The σ2 stress perceived on nouns, adjectives, and numerals pertains regardless of morphological composition, as illustrated below. Exceptions are presented in section 4.1.6. ... Stress falls on this σ2 suffix even though it is an open, light syllable and contributes no meaning or function. ... In contrast to nouns, adjectives, and numerals, verbs are never stressed on σ2. Regardless of their morphological composition, they are stressed on σ1. The most explicit evidence of this contrast is illustrated by minimal pairs ... for instance ... the minimal pair [tʰaq.'pa] thag.pa 'rope' vs. ['tʰaq.pa] 'thag.pa 'to grind…

The secondary Read 1934 'equal emphasis' statement is also present in the held scanned. sources.quote: According to Caplow (2009), “stress has played an important role in the development of tone in Tibetan.” The distinction of stress is attested mainly in Balti. Caplow (2016) and some other scholars believe that Amdo or even Lhasa also have a stress opposition but it may play a secondary role in the system. The distinction of stress only occurs in polysyllabic words. Ex. in Balti: KHUR.BA ‘bread’ /k’urba/ vs. ’KHUR-BA ‘to carry’ /k’urba/; KLAD.PA ‘brain’ /xlatpa/ vs. GLAD-PA ‘to be tired’ /xlatpa/; THAG.PA ‘rope’ /thakpa/ vs. ’THAG-BA /thakpa/ ‘to grind’.
sources.locator: sec. 7.3.3 Stress, printed p. 241; also printed p. 235: 'Amdo, Ladaks, Purik, Zanhar and Balti do not have any distinctive tones'
sources.note: Balti: no distinctive tones; contrastive stress position in polysyllabic (noun vs. verb) pairs; the transcriptions do not mark where the stress falls.balt1258 appears). Balti prosody said to be influenced by Urdu/Persian (printed p. 242).

Comparative paper on the origin of tone in Tibetan dialects; per Caplow 2016 (LTBA 39.2 'Reconstructing stress in Proto-Tibetan', abstract surfaced by web search) Bielmeier argued that stress was one of three basic factors in the development of tonal phenomena in modern Tibetan dialects and that the Western Archaic Tibetan (Balti) stress pattern reflects the oldest ascertainable pre-tonal stage; whether Leh Ladakhi forms are cited is unverified.
